1:
Ellicott notes that Mark alone names the town, where the parallel calls it simply his own city, and that difference is the one problem the older readers work at. Augustine offers two ways out: either Galilee itself may be called the Lord's city, Capernaum being of such standing there as to be reckoned its metropolis, or else the other evangelist passed over everything between the arrival in his own country and the arrival at Capernaum, and joined the paralytic's story straight on. Pseudo-Chrysostom supplies a third and simpler answer — Capernaum was called his city because he went there often and did many miracles there.

Whose house it was draws unusual agreement. Gill names it the house of Simon and Andrew, where he had been before and where he lodged when in Capernaum; Clarke and Wesley both say Peter's; Robertson renders the phrase more exactly as at home, in Peter's house which is now the home of Jesus, and calls the detail another picture coming directly from Peter's own telling.

The interval before the return is measured only loosely. Robertson explains the phrase as days coming in between the departure and the return, without saying how many. Barnes admits the number is unknown and guesses that the stay in the desert lasted long enough to heal those brought to him and to teach the crowds that followed; Gill fills the gap with preaching through Galilee and days of prayer in retirement. Barnes adds a point of geography that removes an apparent difficulty: Capernaum was not the town he had lately been unable to enter openly, so there was nothing to prevent his staying and preaching there. Henry supplies a motive: Christ came back to his headquarters hoping the talk and the crowds had somewhat abated — which the next verse disposes of.

On the crowd itself Henry is the most vivid. They did not wait for the sabbath and the synagogue, where they might be sure of finding him; as soon as it was known he was in town they came, one inviting another, until the house could not hold them. Where the king is, Henry says, there is the court. Robertson reads the same scene through the grammar — the Greek piles negative on negative to say there was no room left even about the door — and infers something about the building: this door apparently opened straight into the street, not into a courtyard as the doors of larger houses did, so the house was packed inside and jammed outside. On that last point Barnes and Clarke take the opposite view, both glossing the phrase about the door as meaning the yard or court in front of the house.

What he did with the crowd is put carefully. Ellicott renders the clause literally as he spake the word. Barnes takes the word to mean the revelation or doctrine Christ came to deliver, and Clarke narrows it to the doctrine of the kingdom of God. Robertson attends to the verb rather than the object: it stands in Mark's favourite descriptive imperfect, so that he was speaking to them, and the word chosen originally meant no more than the chatter of birds or the prattling of children, though it is used here of the most serious speech there is, with some emphasis left on the sound and manner of it.

Two of the witnesses stand back from the scene. Bede observes that the compassion of God does not desert even carnal persons, but grants them the grace of his presence so that they too may be made spiritual; and he marks the movement — after the desert, the Lord returns into the city. Wesley notes what the crowding still meant at this stage: the general impression on their hearts continued, and at Capernaum all who heard were as yet receiving the word with joy.
3:
Two details here belong to Mark and to nobody else, and both close readers say so. Ellicott notes that only Mark gives the number of bearers; Robertson calls the four a picturesque Markan touch absent from the other accounts, and adds that the verb they come stands in Mark's vivid dramatic present, which one parallel keeps and the other flattens. Clarke pictures the arrangement, four men one at each corner of the couch, and infers the man's condition: too feeble to come himself and too weak to be carried otherwise. Gill widens the party beyond the four, supposing a body of townsmen, friends and relations came too.

Why they went up on the roof is agreed. Pseudo-Chrysostom has them find the door blocked by the crowd, so that they could not enter that way at all; hoping the man might yet merit the grace of healing, they raised the bed with its burden, uncovered the roof, and laid him with his bed before the face of the Saviour.

What they actually took apart is disputed, and the answers range from no damage to a good deal. Barnes has them do no structural harm: the roofs were flat and, in a town, joined to their neighbours, so the bearers probably crossed from the next house, and what they removed was the curtain or awning drawn over the central area, with part of the banisters. Wesley allows a little more, taking up the lattice or trap door that every flat-roofed house had and then breaking the opening wider when it proved too narrow for the couch. Clarke goes further again — the trap door was too small, so they stripped off part of the tiles and took away the laths and timber the tiles were fastened to. Robertson is the most physical: they climbed an outside stair to the flat tiled roof and dug out the covering, which was not thin — laths and plaster with slabs of stone set in for strength. The Greek says, with a play on words, that they unroofed the roof, a verb found nowhere else in the New Testament and rare in late Greek. Ellicott settles the degree from the language: the strong expressions for the injury done to the roof are peculiar to Mark, where the parallel says only through the tiles.

Where in the house Jesus was sitting is left open. Barnes puts him in the large open hall at the centre, with the crowd filling that area and blocking the door. Robertson declines to choose, listing downstairs, upstairs and the quadrangle as the three possibilities and saying plainly that it is not clear. He quotes a description of such roofs that explains why digging was needed — mortar, tar, ashes and sand rolled hard, with grass in the crevices and goats cropping it on country houses.

Lightfoot supplies what the act would have meant to Jewish readers, and it is not flattering. The rabbis knew the phrase the way of the roof: when one teacher died and his bier proved too wide for the door, his household proposed to lower it through the roof, and another rebuked them: it redounds to the honour of a wise man to be carried out by the door. The same phrase turns up in the schools as a legal question — whether a man enters his house by the gate or by the way of the roof — in a case concerning a building whose lower part the owner occupies while the upper is let to another.

Ellicott closes on the bed itself. Mark does not use the word the first Gospel uses, but the Greek form of a Latin one, the pallet or camp bed of the poor; the same word appears twice elsewhere in the New Testament and never in either of the other two accounts.
5:
Whose faith Jesus saw is disputed three ways. Pseudo-Chrysostom is definite that it was not the sick man's but his bearers', and states the principle openly — it sometimes happens that a man is healed by the faith of another. Gill and Robertson both include the paralytic, Robertson adding that there is no reason to exclude him. Bede takes the middle case: one may see how much a man's own faith weighs with God when another's had such force that a whole man rose up healed in body and soul, and by one man's merit another had his sins forgiven.

The word of address is weighed carefully. Barnes points out that the term is literally child, used by the Hebrews with great latitude, and that here it carries affection: a word of consolation meant to show compassion and inspire confidence. Bede hears something sharper in it, that Christ's humility calls a despised and broken man his son when the priests would not deign to touch him;.

That the forgiveness came first, and instead of the healing, is the point the ancients and the moderns converge on. Robertson calls it the astonishing thing to the paralytic and the four alike, and suggests the sins had caused the paralysis. Bede argues the order theologically: the Lord loosed the chains of the man's sins first, to show that his joints had been unstrung because of those bonds and could not be healed until they were loosed. Chrysostom makes the sequence an argument rather than a diagnosis — he first healed the soul, which is what he came to seek, so that when they doubted he could bring forward a visible work and let it confirm his word, a hidden sign proved by an open one.

The objectors are introduced with some care. Robertson reads the scene as another picture from Peter's eyes: they were there to pick flaws, and though there is no evidence they said anything aloud, the debate in their hearts was written on their faces: no sound had come, but feeling had. Ellicott notes that the better manuscripts break the sentence in two, so that the charge stands bare: why doth this Man thus speak? He blasphemeth. Bede supplies what the charge was worth in law — they were anticipating the sentence of his death, since the Law commanded that a blasphemer be put to death.

Wesley alone turns on the objectors directly. See whence the first offence cometh, he writes: not one of the plain unlettered people had been offended, and all rejoiced in the light until these men of learning came to put darkness for light; and prays that his own tongue may cleave to his mouth before he offends one of God's simple ones.

Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic background to the objection. He quotes a dispute in which a heretic presses Rabh Idith on the angel who bears the divine name, and asks what is meant by the text saying he will not forgive your sins; the rabbi answers that this is true, and that they therefore did not receive him even as a messenger. The assumption on both sides is the one the scribes make here, that pardon belongs to God alone. Lightfoot's own comment is directed at the rabbis: you rejected the very one in whom the name was, and to your own great mischief.

On how Jesus knew their thoughts the witnesses pull opposite ways. Gill insists the spirit here is neither the human soul nor the Holy Spirit, though both might be called his, but the divine nature by which he knew all things, including men's secret thoughts. Ellicott finds the opposite significance in the same phrase: the naming of the spirit as the region of our Lord's consciousness is peculiar to Mark, and bears on the reality and completeness of his human nature.
9:
The question which is easier proves harder than it looks, and the witnesses answer it three ways. Lightfoot recovers the idiom: in the Jewish schools, and the schoolmen were standing right there, easy and hard describe a sense that is plain or obscure rather than an act that is simple or difficult. On that reading the clause should run, it is easier to say thy sins are forgiven thee than to say rise up and walk — easier because nobody in the room could check it. Theophylact puts the same insight into the Pharisees' mouths: they thought healing a body the harder thing, being open to view, and curing a soul the easier, the cure being invisible, so a man who could do more would have mended the body instead of retreating into what cannot be seen. What the Saviour does, on Theophylact's account, is prove the harder by the easier — the health of the soul, which is really more difficult, by the healing of the body, which is really less so though it looked otherwise to them.

Pseudo-Chrysostom states the logic of the next move. Because it is easier to say a thing than to do it, there was still something to be said in objection while the work remained unperformed; so he adds, that ye may know: since you doubt my word, I will bring on a work that confirms what you could not see. Robertson reaches the same place from the other end: either sentence would have been equally futile from the scribes and equally effective from Jesus, who took the harder first, the forgiveness nobody could verify, and then did the thing everyone could watch.

The title he claims in doing it is noticed by both Gill and Robertson. Gill takes Son of man to mean himself, really man and the true Messiah, the phrase having been so used already in the older scriptures. Robertson calls it Christ's favourite designation of himself, a messianic claim in terms that could not easily be attacked, and presses what goes with it: authority to forgive sins here on earth, now, without waiting for the day of judgment.

Robertson also finds a piece of evidence in an oddity of construction. The narrative breaks off mid-sentence to say he saith to the sick of the palsy, and that same parenthesis stands at that same point in all three Gospels — which he takes as proof that the other two followed Mark's account, since it is inconceivable that three writers should independently insert the same aside in the same place.

Lightfoot points out that before them all can as truly be rendered against them all, and pictures the crowd so packed that there was no way through, so that the man, now not merely whole but strong and lusty, pressed through and made his way out stoutly with his bed on his shoulders. Robertson notes that one parallel keeps the detail, and that the proceeding saved Jesus arguing with the scribes further. Barnes glosses the crowd's words as meaning simply that they had never seen anything like it, and Ellicott compares the reports: one parallel gives the substance without the words, the other has them say they had seen strange things that day.

Two of the readers take the paralysis as a figure. Pseudo-Jerome makes it a type of the torpor in which a man lies slothful in the softness of the flesh while still desiring health. Clarke quotes Prosper to the same effect — sin being a grovelling on the earth followed by a universal palsy of the soul, an inability to break off its habits or take one good step toward God; and grace, being nothing but the almighty will of God, who does whatever he commands, can repair the whole of it in a moment.
13:
Why he went out to the water is answered four ways, and they are not incompatible. Henry says he went for room, having found by a second trial that no house or street would hold the crowd, and draws a rare inference: our Lord must have had a strong voice and used it, since the shore has no walls to help a speaker. Robertson makes it smaller and more human — a walk Jesus loved, taken as soon as he could get clear of the packed house — and notes what followed, that the crowd came again and he taught them rather than escaping. Theophylact turns the same sequence into a maxim about fame: he went to the sea as though wishing to be alone, and the crowd ran after him, so that one may learn that the more you flee from glory the more she pursues, and if you chase her she flies. Bede finds a purpose in the place itself: that he might order the life not only of townsmen but of those living by the sea, and teach them to despise the restless motion of things that pass away like waves and to master it by firmness of faith. Gill and Barnes name the water as the lake beside which Capernaum stood, and Wesley notes that he taught them there as readily as if they had been in a synagogue.

That the man called here is the evangelist under another name is agreed, and three of the witnesses say why it matters. Chrysostom lays out the usage — Matthew in his own book, simply Levi in one parallel, Levi the son of Alphaeus in this one — and reaches for a precedent, that two names are common enough in scripture, as the father-in-law of Moses is called now Jethro and now Raguel. Bede presses it hard. The other two evangelists, he says, out of reverence for a fellow apostle, decline to attach the notorious name to him, while Matthew in his own Gospel accuses himself, setting down Matthew and publican together; and Bede gives that self-accusation a purpose: no convert should despair when a man could be changed in a moment from a tax-farmer into an apostle.

What the man was sitting at is explained from both ends. Bede gives the word its Greek and Latin equivalents and defines it as the place where customs are looked after and administered. Robertson gives the geography and the politics: a toll-gate on the great west road from Damascus to the Mediterranean, its keeper collecting for Herod Antipas, and the whole class of them hated by the Jews and lumped in with sinners.

The speed of the call is what strikes the readers. Robertson calls the challenge sudden and sharp and the response immediate, and observes that great decisions are often made on a moment's notice, adding that Levi is a fine object lesson for men of business who put off service to Christ until their affairs allow it. Pseudo-Jerome reads the name itself as the point, Levi meaning Appointed, and has him follow out of the custom-house of human affairs the Word who said that a man who does not quit all he has cannot be a disciple. Bede reduces the whole matter to four words: to follow is to imitate. Theophylact measures the change by its first effect: the man who lived by plotting against others becomes so benevolent that he fills his house with guests.

Henry closes with a genealogy that, if it holds, makes the call a family affair. This Levi was the son of the Alphaeus also called Cleophas, whose wife Mary was sister or near kinswoman to the mother of Jesus; on that reckoning he was own brother to James the less, Jude and Simon the Canaanite, so that four brothers stood among the apostles.
15:
The dinner is placed and explained without difficulty. Gill sets it in Levi's own house in the town, not the toll booth he had just walked away from, and reads it as an entertainment offered in gratitude. Barnes points out that the words at meat are not in the Greek at all, the phrase meaning simply that he reclined at the meal, and credits the feast to Matthew as an honour done to the Saviour. Robertson calls it a great reception.

Who else was there, and why, divides the accounts a little. Wesley supposes some were invited by Matthew out of compassion for his old companions in sin, but reads the clause about there being many as implying that most of them waited for no invitation and simply pressed in after Jesus, keeping as close to him as they could. Robertson agrees and sharpens it: they did not merely accept Levi's invitation but imitated his example and were following Jesus — a motley crew, as he says, in the eyes of the young theologues who had come to watch. Barnes takes the same clause as evidence about the ministry at large: Jesus was at this stage extremely popular, and became unpopular among common people only after the rich and the great had ridiculed him.

What the word sinners meant is a straight disagreement. Lightfoot answers it from the rabbinic lists and names the trades: dicers, usurers, plunderers, publicans, herdsmen of the lesser cattle, men who sold the produce of the seventh year. On that reckoning the company was Jewish and disreputable by Jewish reckoning. Clarke takes the Greek word to mean the Gentiles or heathen, on the ground that the Jews never applied the term to any of themselves. Robertson stands between: it was an offence for a Jew to eat with Gentiles at all, and publicans and sinners were regarded much as Gentiles were, so the objection would have been the same either way.

Robertson also places the objectors physically. The correct text calls them the scribes of the Pharisees, and he pictures them either in the long hall of the house or, more likely, outside it, too pious to enter a publican's door. Wesley notes the shift in the opposition, the men of learning now joined by the saints of the world and going further in raising prejudice; and he notes that Christ uses no harshness yet, only calm and dispassionate reasoning. Theophylact puts the Pharisees' posture in a phrase — they blame this, making themselves pure. Clarke adds a textual detail that changes the tone of the complaint: a number of good manuscripts and versions, with two of the Fathers, make them ask not how is it that he eateth but why doth your Master eat, addressing the disciples rather than muttering about him.

The reply raises a textual question of its own. Clarke reports that the closing words unto repentance are absent from a long list of manuscripts and versions, that Griesbach struck them from the text and several other editors approved, and that the parallel account retains them in every copy. Robertson agrees they are not genuine here. Clarke then argues from sense as well as evidence: properly speaking the righteous cannot be called to repentance, having already forsaken sin and turned to God.

On the word righteous itself Robertson observes that Jesus grants the Pharisees their claim for the sake of the argument, though elsewhere he shows them to be extortionate and hypocritical, and that granting it is precisely what stops their mouths: the strong are not the people who need a physician in an epidemic. Ellicott notices what Mark leaves out — the citation from the older scriptures that stands in the parallel — and takes the omission, here as elsewhere, for a mark of a Gospel written with Gentile readers in view.
18:
The Gloss notices the symmetry of the two attacks: first the Master was accused to the disciples for keeping company with sinners at table, and now the disciples are complained of to the Master for neglecting fasts — the point, as the Gloss reads it, being to raise matter for dissension between them. Henry sees the same shape: Christ had been made to justify himself, and now must justify them, which he will always do where they act according to his will. Why it came at that moment is a matter of the calendar: Robertson notes that Levi's feast probably fell on one of the weekly fast-days kept by stricter Jews, so that two standpoints collided over one dinner, and Gill suspects the same.

Augustine works on a discrepancy in who did the asking. One account has John's disciples alone put the question, while Mark adds the Pharisees; and Augustine finds the solution in the wording that follows, since they came and say to him implies people arriving rather than the same men already described as fasting. His reconstruction is that guests who remembered the fast came over, the apostles being present too, and each objected as eagerly as he could.

What lay behind the question is read unkindly by three of the witnesses. Chrysostom makes it jealousy, the questioners wanting to know whether he alone of all men, with his followers, could win the fight against the passions without abstinence and toil. Theophylact is gentler about John's disciples, who were in an imperfect state and continued in Jewish custom; Robertson agrees they sided with the Pharisees in ceremonial observance, and adds that John, still a prisoner, was the greater ascetic of the two, and that neither he nor Jesus satisfied the popular critics.

The answer turns on a figure, and its terms are examined closely. Robertson observes that sons of the bridechamber means not merely the groomsmen but the wedding guests, and that Jesus is taking up the Baptist's own image and altering it — the friend of the bridegroom becoming the sons of the bridechamber — while identifying himself with the bridegroom of the older scriptures, God in covenant with his people. Mourning, Robertson says, does not suit a wedding feast. Pseudo-Chrysostom takes the betrothal forward to the Church: it is the giving of an earnest, namely the grace of the Spirit by which the world believed. Theophylact adds why the figure fits this season — the time of the first coming is not one of sorrow but of rest, salvation coming without the works of the law.

Lest that be mistaken for licence, Pseudo-Chrysostom points to the clause that follows. The days will come, and when the Bridegroom is taken away they will fast, longing for his return and uniting their spirits to him by bodily suffering; so their present freedom is a circumstance and not a rule. Clarke adds a textual variant with a sharp point: many of the best manuscripts read in that day rather than in those days, meaning the day of the betrayal, and Griesbach adopted it, though Clarke thinks the first half of the verse tells for the common reading.

Two of the older readers turn the whole exchange inward. Theophylact makes every man of good works a son of the Bridegroom, who has Christ with him and does not fast, that is, does no works of repentance because he is not sinning; and when the Bridegroom is taken by a fall into sin, he fasts and repents to cure it. Bede reads the fasting party the same way: the man who boasts of works without faith and takes in the preaching of Christ by the ear and not the heart wastes with a fasting soul, while the man joined to the members of Christ by faithful love cannot fast, since he feasts on the Body and the Blood.
21:
Who the old garments and old bottles stand for is the one substantial disagreement here, and it runs in opposite directions. Bede and Theophylact both apply them to the disciples themselves. Theophylact says they are likened to old garments because of the infirmity of their minds, on which it was not fitting to lay the heavy command of fasting. Bede says the same of the bottles — they would have burst at spiritual precepts rather than be held in by them — and then carries the figure forward: they will be new bottles after the ascension, renewed by longing for his consolation, and then the new wine will come to them, the fervour of the Spirit filling the hearts of spiritual men. Gill applies both to the other party altogether. The old bottles are the scribes and Pharisees, the whole who needed no physician and the righteous Christ did not come to call; and the new wine is the love of God, or the blessings of the new covenant, or the gospel that reports them, none of which such men receive.

Gill also identifies the new cloth, and identifies it with the very thing under dispute: the traditions of the elders about eating and drinking and fasting, which occasioned the parable in the first place. He presses the irony in calling them new — they were novelties beside the commands of God, some of very recent devising and most, if not all, later than the time of Ezra.

Bede draws two rules of teaching out of the same image. A teacher must not commit the hidden things of the new mysteries to a soul hardened in old wickedness; and it was not yet fitting to sew on the new piece, meaning a portion of doctrine that requires a general fast from all the joy of temporal things, since to do that is to tear the teaching so that it no longer agrees with the old.

The rest of the attention is textual and lexical. Robertson notes that the verb for sewing on occurs here and nowhere else, in the New Testament or outside it, though the simple verb is common enough, and that both parallels use a different compound meaning rather to clap a patch on. Clarke observes that the common printed editions open the verse with a conjunction which almost every manuscript and version of note omits, and that the construction varies considerably among the copies. Barnes glosses the cloth as raw or unwrought rather than merely new. And on the closing clause about new wine in fresh skins, Robertson reports that Westcott and Hort bracket it as a Western non-interpolation, though it is dropped by only one manuscript and some old Latin copies, and that since it is certainly genuine in the parallel it may well be genuine here too.
23:
What the disciples were actually doing is described with some care. Barnes explains that corn here means grain of the wheat and barley kind and never maize, and pictures them gathering as they walked and rubbing the heads to shell them. Robertson works on Mark's verbs for a different picture: the word means to go along beside, so they were perhaps now on the edge of the field and now inside it, and a second phrase means to make a way, as if through standing grain; the Revised margin, he says, has it right — they began to make their way plucking the ears. He adds the detail that decides the case: the rabbis classed this as preparing food.

Why they were doing it is agreed. Chrysostom says they ate simple food, not for pleasure but from necessity of nature, and that the Pharisees, serving the figure and the shadow, made an accusation of it. Barnes draws a lesson from the circumstance rather than the act: although the Lord was with them and had all things at his disposal, he let them supply their want this way.

Augustine supplies the legal point that shows what was and was not charged. Israel had a written precept that a thief found in the fields was not to be detained unless he tried to carry something off; a man who touched nothing but what he ate went free. So the disciples were within the law of property, and the accusation had to be sabbath-breaking rather than theft.

Calvin makes the same observation and turns it into a rule of interpretation. The Pharisees do not blame them for taking from a field not their own, but for violating the sabbath, as though famishing men ought rather to die than satisfy their hunger. The sabbath was given so that the people, sanctifying themselves to God, might be employed in spiritual worship, and, free of worldly occupations, might attend the holy assemblies; and its lawful observation must be measured against that purpose, since a law ought to be interpreted according to the design of the Lawgiver. Calvin will not let the motive pass: what he sees is the implacable nature of superstition and the cruelty of hypocrites once ambition is joined to hatred of the person. Barnes notes more coolly that the act was lawful under Moses without distinction of days, and that the Pharisees had invented the exception Christ now answers out of their own law.

Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the scene as the freedom of men past the figure. The disciples, released from the shadow and joined to the truth, do not keep the figurative feast; and the precedent of David, who ate what the law forbade when he touched the priests' food, is produced to cancel the charge. What lies behind the precedent, he says, is the title claimed at the end: the law has no authority over the Lawgiver, and more is allowed a king than is appointed to other men. He notes too that the one calling himself Lord of the sabbath calls himself Son of man in the same breath, the Son of God having deigned to be so named for men's sake.

One difficulty in the precedent is raised by one witness and answered by another. Theophylact asks how the evangelist can call Abiathar high priest at that moment when the older history names Abimelech. Bede's solution is that both men were present when David came for the bread — Abimelech the high priest and Abiathar his son — and that Abiathar, after his father was killed by Saul, fled to David and shared his exile, coming to the office himself when David came to the throne. The son so far outgrew the father, on Bede's reckoning, that he could properly be named as high priest even of an occasion in his father's lifetime.
26:
Lightfoot returns to the difficulty about the priest's name with something quite unlike the usual defences. He knows the standard answer, that the father bore both names and so did the son, but thinks more was intended. Among the Jews the name Abiathar stood by association for the Urim and Thummim, since under the father and son of that name the inquiring by that oracle is mentioned more often than anywhere else, and after the son scarcely at all. On that reading the phrase in the days of Abiathar the high priest is not a dating but a claim about authority: David had his bread from a priest who had the oracle with him and was acting under divine direction. The precedent is then not an irregularity excused but a decision properly made.

Gill fixes the place: the house of God here is the tabernacle, the temple not being built yet, and David came on a sabbath, the day when the old loaves were taken away and divided among the priests. From that Gill draws his application: those hungering and thirsting after righteousness should go where there is bread enough and to spare, and the day set apart for public worship is the day for going.

The saying that follows is treated by Barnes and Henry as the governing principle of the whole dispute, and they state it in almost the same terms. Henry calls the sabbath a privilege rather than a drudgery: God never designed it to be a burden, and we must not make it one to ourselves. Barnes sets out what it was designed to do — rest from toil, relief from the cares of the world, undisturbed time to seek the consolations of religion — and argues from consequences, that where the day is not kept there is ignorance and vice and disorder, and where it is kept order prevails and the poor are raised in their condition. Both men then press the second clause. Barnes makes it a matter of sequence: man was made first and the sabbath appointed afterwards for his welfare, not the sabbath first and man made with reference to it; so a law intended for man's good must not be interpreted against it. Henry gets there another way: man was not made for the sabbath as though his keeping it could be of service to God, so every observance of it is to be interpreted by the rule of mercy.

The closing title is where the readings divide. Gill takes the Son of man to be Christ himself, claiming power not merely to dispense with the sabbath but to abrogate it as he did the rest of the ceremonial law, so that the Pharisees had no business objecting to what was done with his leave. Robertson notes a word Mark alone supplies, lord even of the sabbath, and reads it as a sign of how large a claim Jesus knew he was making. Clarke reports a rival interpretation, that the phrase means man in general, any man being lord of a sabbath made for his own ease and use. He rejects it as at once harsh and lax, since on that reading a man might make what use he pleased of the day and the moral obligation would soon be gone. In its place Clarke puts purpose rather than ownership: the ordinances of religion are regulated by their end, the honour of God and the salvation of men, and it belongs to true religion to contain nothing that is not beneficial to man. God required the rest, he says, so that servants should not be oppressed by their masters, that the labouring beasts might rest, and that men might attend upon his ordinances — which shows he asks worship neither out of indigence nor interest, but out of goodness, to make men happy.
